newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eramet raises the stakes in N.Caledonia row.
newsitem.headline: Eramet raises the stakes in N.Caledonia row.

text.p: Nickel producer Eramet on Tuesday upped the stakes in its dispute with France over the distribution of mining assets in New-Caledonia.
Amid mounting speculation over the removal of chairman Yves Rambaud, the nine members of Eramet's management committee publicly stated their support for the embattled chairman.
They also rejected criticism made by state holding company Erap, which owns the state's 55 percent stake in Ermemt, against the way Eramet had handled the mining row.

In a letter to Erap's president Remy Chardon nine top officials representing Eramet and its units Societe le Nickel and Erasteel said the attacks were "unfounded" and the method used "particularly shocking".
Chardon, who joined Eramet's board on April 16, had blamed Eramet's managers for having wasted an "enormous amount of time" in the dispute.
Industry sources said the managers took the unual step of making their reaction public in a show of solidarity towards Rambaud, the main target of Erap's wrath.

Erap, which controls 55 percent of Eramet capital, has said it wants control of Eramet's board at the next shareholders' meeting on May 28. The move that may herald the replacement of Rambaud, who has opposed any plans to curb Eramet's development strategy in New Caledonia.

"What is important is that the top officials of Eramet's main units signed the letter. This means that if Rambaud goes, all top management will have to go," one source said. He added that this prospect would make any contender think twice before accepting Rambaud's job.

The departure of Rambaud, who is highly regarded by investors and analysts, will also not go down well with minority shareholders, notably investment funds, who have strongly criticised the government role in the conflict.
Sources said this could have serious consequences for future privatisations, notably the sale of France Telecom.
Erap may release on Wednesday the list of the candidates it wants to put on Eramet's board, including the name of a possible successor for Rambaud, they said.
The French state and Eramet have been involved in a dispute over controversial plans to build a new nickel smelter in the north of New Caledonia.
The government wants to use some of Eramet's mining reserves to supply the future plant of Canadian group Falconbrige and local Kanak company Societe Miniere de Sud Pacifique (SMSP).
Government support for the project aimed at appeasing Kanak separatists ahead of a 1998 referendum on independence.
Eramet has repeatedly stated it does not oppose the plan as long as it did not threaten its existing projects in the South-Pacific island.

After several months of deadlock, Eramet, Erap, Falconbridge and SMSP, met last Friday to discuss the project and in a joint statement they said they had found common ground and that experts would be brought in to work on the remaing problems.
Erap said the meeting had been "very positive" and that it hoped for an agreement soon. But analysts said that even if an accord came through many issues remained unsolved.
"Even if there is an agreement with SMSP, this will not solve the political problems in New Caledonia," an analyst said.
He explained that SMSP was controlled by only one of the many separatist factions on the island and that investors were worried over future disruptions to the mines and nickel exports.

Analysts said that even if Eramet got a financial compensation for helping supply the new smelter, this would not make up for lost production which could eventually lead to plant closures and job cuts in New Caledonia and in France, they said.
